title: An open LLM read 291 retracted papers: 7.7% of passages mention the retraction
content:
Officially corrected errors persist in AI training data: Céphéide public alert, data and proofs
Description
Version 1.2 (31 October 2026). Four folders added, measurements made on 30 October 2026 in the continuation of step S1: does OLMo 2, an open model whose training data are public, say that a paper is retracted when its data said so? Result: in what the model read about 291 retracted papers it had seen often, 7.7 % of the passages mention the retraction; the model said "retracted" for none of the 891 papers asked (S4 and S5) and "not retracted" for 425, but it does not know these papers (correct journal: 2 / 891), so no conclusion is drawn on the model. Preregistered, sealed and anchored in Bitcoin before the first question. See README — v1.2.md. The files of version 1.1 and the article arXiv:2610.34379 are unchanged.
Version 1.2 (31 octobre 2026). Quatre dossiers ajoutés, des mesures faites le 30 octobre 2026 dans la suite de l'étape S1 : OLMo 2, un modèle ouvert dont les données d'entraînement sont publiques, dit-il qu'un article est rétracté quand ses données le disaient ? Résultat : dans ce que le modèle a lu sur 291 articles rétractés qu'il avait vus souvent, 7,7 % des passages mentionnent la rétractation ; le modèle n'a dit « rétracté » pour aucun des 891 articles interrogés (S4 et S5) et « pas rétracté » pour 425, mais il ne connaît pas ces articles (revue juste : 2 / 891) : on ne conclut pas sur le modèle. Préenregistré, scellé et ancré dans Bitcoin avant la première question. Voir LISEZ-MOI — v1.2.md. Les fichiers de la version 1.1 et l'article arXiv:2610.34379 sont inchangés.
Public alert by Céphéide, Loxyn's measurement bench, with all data, scripts, readings and proofs. French and English texts of the alert are in ALERTE/; the step-by-step guide is README.md (English) and 00 — LISEZ-MOI.md (French). Article: arXiv:2610.34379. The full package (every step folder, lists, proofs) is in the zip file; MANIFESTE.sha256 gives the SHA-256 of each file it contains.
Official texts are corrected after publication: EU corrigenda in the Official Journal, verified RFC errata, retractions of scientific papers. We measured whether these corrections are present in public datasets used to train language models (EurlexResources, FineWeb-2, a FineWeb sample, peS2o) and what models answer about the corrected passages. Main results: 95.5% of testable single-language corrections to EU acts (1,989/2,082) remain in their erroneous form in EurlexResources; at least 124 corrected EU-law errors and 60 verified RFC errata are reproduced in web training data; about 12,200 retracted papers are in peS2o, 79% with no mention of the retraction; 53% of a random sample of retracted papers are still cited a year or more after retraction (OpenAlex); asked without documents, five models give the erroneous version in 45% of the answers in which they commit to one version, and one answer in 295 says it does not know. Shown both versions side by side, the models choose the corrected one in 53% of cases, and naming the act makes no difference; when each version carries its date and the corrigendum label, the four larger models choose it in 99–100% of cases.
Every step was preregistered and its fingerprints timestamped with OpenTimestamps in the Bitcoin blockchain. Failed controls, lost bets and deviations are reported. The Retraction Watch file is not redistributed (its SHA-256 is in the seal of the retraction step).
Version 1.1 (27 October 2026): adds README.md, the English translation of 00 — LISEZ-MOI.md, and the link to the article on arXiv. No other file has changed.

report.summary: An open audit finds corrections and retractions largely missing from public LLM training data, and open models rarely reproduce the corrected record.
report.background: Web-scale training corpora are snapshots of a literature that is constantly revised: EU acts get corrigenda in the Official Journal, technical standards get verified errata, and journals retract papers. Scraped datasets rarely ingest those later corrections, so models can learn the original, wrong version and never see the fix. The Céphéide alert, produced with Loxyn's measurement bench, tests this directly across EurlexResources, FineWeb-2, a FineWeb sample and peS2o, plus the fully open OLMo 2 model whose training data is public. Unusually for AI claims, each step was preregistered, fingerprinted with OpenTimestamps and anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain before the first question was asked, and the authors publish failed controls, lost bets and deviations alongside the results. The accompanying preprint is arXiv:2610.34379.
key_points: OLMo 2 read about 291 retracted papers frequently enough to have seen them, but only 7.7% of the passages it consumed about them actually mention the retraction. The model's public training data therefore carry mostly silent retractions rather than flagged ones.

In a preregistered probe of 891 papers, OLMo 2 never answered "retracted" and said "not retracted" for 425. But it could not name the correct journal for more than 2 of 891, so the authors explicitly refuse to draw conclusions about the model itself.

Corrections to official texts survive poorly in corpora: 95.5% of testable single-language EU corrigenda (1,989 of 2,082) remain in their erroneous form in EurlexResources, and at least 124 corrected EU-law errors plus 60 verified RFC errata reappear in web training data.

On retractions, peS2o holds roughly 12,200 retracted papers, 79% with no mention of the retraction, and OpenAlex data show 53% of a random sample are still cited a year or more after being retracted — the error propagates through the citation graph into text.

Answer behavior depends heavily on framing: asked without documents, five models give the erroneous version in 45% of answers where they commit (only 1 in 295 admits ignorance); shown both versions side by side they pick the corrected one 53% of the time, but with dates and a corrigendum label the four larger models choose it 99–100% of the time.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report reframes data quality from a filtering problem into a versioning problem: deduplication and toxicity filters do not catch a stale corrigendum, and scale does not fix it. Teams building legal, medical or scientific assistants should assume their corpus contains superseded claims and add retrieval over authoritative, dated sources rather than relying on parametric memory. For developers, the striking result is the prompt-sensitivity gap — 53% to 99% purely from labeling versions and dates — which suggests cheap, high-leverage interventions in how sources are presented. For regular users, the practical takeaway is that a confident answer may be an outdated one, and that citations and dates, not fluency, are the signal to trust.
report.tools: The full package — data, scripts, readings and SHA-256 manifest — is on Zenodo (record 23830104), with the preprint at arXiv:2610.34379. To reproduce or extend: OLMo 2 and its Dolma corpus for open training-data inspection, peS2o and FineWeb-2 for corpus sampling, EurlexResources for legal texts, the Retraction Watch database (hash-sealed, not redistributed here) and OpenAlex for citation tracking. OpenTimestamps is useful if you want your own preregistered results sealed in Bitcoin.
